case_title: Rajesh Bhatnagar v. State of Uttarakhand
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse (husband Mukesh Bhatnagar); Relative (brother-in-law Rajesh Bhatnagar and mother-in-law, co-accused)
evidence_type: Ocular (PW1 uncle, PW2 mother), medical (post-mortem and injury evidence), documentary (letters written by the deceased), recovery of articles from the scene, circumstantial
aggravating_circumstances: Death within seven years of marriage; persistent dowry demands; beatings and cruelty; brutal manner; false defence; absconding after the death
mitigating_circumstances: None noted (defence argued youth of accused and age of their mother; Court found no mitigating circumstances)
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.304-B IPC; life imprisonment for all three accused
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and life sentence confirmed
neutral_facts: The victim married the accused husband in May 1994 after an engagement during which the accused family demanded a refrigerator; the victim's family paid Rs.10,000 before the engagement ceremony was completed. After the marriage the accused demanded a television and a cooler, and the victim told her family she was beaten for not bringing them. She was sent back to her parental home and later returned to the matrimonial home after relatives gave an assurance; when leaving she said she feared her in-laws would kill her. In February 1996 a relative received a call that an accident had befallen the victim. The victim's mother and uncle went to the matrimonial home and learnt that she had been sprinkled with kerosene and set on fire for failing to bring the television and cooler. The victim's mother lodged a written complaint the same day. Police found the house open and the accused absent. At the scene police recovered a kerosene container, an empty container smelling of kerosene, burnt ash, a cloth rope, broken bangles and the victim's clothing. The post-mortem showed first and second degree burns over the whole body and death from ante-mortem injuries and shock. The accused husband had about twelve abrasions and contusions. The defence explanation was that he was hurt trying to break open a kitchen door during a stove fire; no burn injury was found on him and no cooking material was found in the kitchen. Letters written by the victim described beatings and cruelty.
physical_harm: Death of the victim by burning (first and second degree burns over the whole body) and ante-mortem injuries and shock; accused husband had about twelve abrasions and contusions
financial_property_loss: Rs.10,000 paid to accused for a refrigerator demanded at engagement
motive: Dowry demands for a refrigerator, television and cooler, which the victim's family could not meet
key_evidence_accepted: Consistent ocular testimony of PW1 (uncle) and PW2 (mother) and the complaint lodged on the day; the victim's letters read with that testimony; post-mortem evidence of burns; recovery of kerosene containers and burnt articles; injuries on accused without burns; trial court's reasons on the false stove-accident defence
witness_credibility: PW2 gave the same complete account in the police report and on oath; PW1 fully corroborated her; no contradiction or variation found
post_offence_conduct: Accused absconded and left the house open after the death; Court treated this as indicating guilt
trial_duration: offence: 17 February 1996 (complaint lodged that day; date of death not separately given); trial judgment: 2 December 1996; High Court: 14 October 2009; Supreme Court: 10 May 2012
legal_representation: Accused: Dinesh Kumar Garg, Meha Aggarwal, Ashutosh Garg. State: S.S. Shamshery, Rahul Verma, Abhishek Atrey, Jatinder Kumar Bhatia
investigation_status: FIR registered; investigation completed; charge sheet filed; trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.304-B and sentenced to life imprisonment. High Court: appeal dismissed. Supreme Court: appeals dismissed
prosecution_argument: Not separately recorded; the prosecution case was that the accused burnt the victim for failing to meet dowry demands, and the Court accepted that case
defence_argument: Ingredients of s.304-B not satisfied because the letters did not mention dowry; no proximity between the refrigerator demand and the death; injuries were sustained in trying to rescue the victim; accidental stove fire; youth of accused and age of mother warranted a lesser sentence
legal_principle_applied: Three ingredients of s.304-B (death within seven years of marriage otherwise than in normal circumstances; cruelty or harassment soon before death; connection with dowry demand); presumption of causation under s.113-B Evidence Act; proximity test for 'soon before'; adverse inference from false plea
precedent_relied_upon: Bansi Lal v. State of Haryana (2011) 11 SCC 359 (relied on); Biswajit Halder v. State of West Bengal (2008) 1 SCC 202 (relied on); Kundula Bala Subrahmanyam v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993) 2 SCC 684 (relied on); Asraf Ali v. State of Assam (2008) 16 SCC 328 (referred); Hemchand v. State of Haryana (1994) 6 SCC 727 (referred); Meka Ramaswamy and Rajesh Tandon (cited)
sentencing_rationale: Brutal manner of offence; committed for satisfaction of dowry demands for television or cooler; false defence of accidental death; no mitigating circumstances, so life imprisonment upheld
judicial_aggravating_factors: Brutal manner of killing; dowry motive (television or cooler); false defence claiming accidental death
